The report finds that, contrary to current recommendations, dietary standards are inadequate for controlling the nutritional content of foods consumed in the U.S., including food items with high intakes of micronutrients such as vitamin C, magnesium, potassium, iron, manganese and iron. Kowalski is working on a long-term study of the sea’s effects on coral reef systems.
The new research was conducted by Professor Jian Gordino, a graduate student in the Marine Science Program at the University of New South Wales, Australia.
Professor Kowalski has been studying corals to analyze the impacts of climate change on coral reefs. He is currently focusing on how global warming affects coral reefs and what we can do about it.
“We want to know if coral reefs are actually changing in response to changes in sea temperatures or future events,” says Professor Gordino, who is also involved in the project. “And we need to understand how different these changes might affect coral reefs.”
“This study shows that changes in ocean circulation may affect the size of the coral reefs,” he says. “It could be because these changes were influenced by changes in land surface temperature, which could cause algal blooms that were not affected by the changes in sea levels. But this could be due to the changes in water pressure caused by climate change.”
